THE MARCH OF THE LAND GIRLS.-A big recruiting rally for women land workers was held on Tuesday, March 19, when a meeting was held in Trafalgar-square. Afterwards between 400 and 500 land lasses marched to Buckingham Palace to be inspected by the Queen. The motor-plough girls looked especially smart.

SUPER COWGRILS AT WORK.
Patrietic efforts to help Farmers.

A party of merry faced women, in jorsoys short, skirts and leavings, have created a big stir at certain Essex fares, where they are employed to replace farmhands who have answered their country's call. These women are working on the land out of sheer patience, and doing it unenommenly well. They look after the feeding of the cattle, clean put the cowsheds, and do all kinds of farm work. A pretty coworker carrying water for the cows. She does not mind the mass of mud.

Owing to the great shortage of male labour women commissionaires are the latest acquisition to the staff of large business establishments.
"Attending a customer arriving by Taxi to make her purchases.
GLASGOW OWEN DOING THEIRFULL SHARE TO WAR WORK--REPDACING MEN AT A DAIRY.

Another branch of war work which the women of Glasgow are tackling. They are seen at a large depot of the Scottish Farmer's Dairy Company, where they do all the heavy tasks previously performed by men, such as loading the vans, cleaning the cans and tipping the milk into the tanks. Our photo shows.At the refrigerator.
FIRST WOMAN INSURANCE BROKER.

Miss Lilian H.Tutcher, the first woman insurance broker,who has started business as director and manager of a Queen Victoria-Street firm, interviewing a client. She has had five years' experience as the City manager of a leading firm of Lloyd's brokers. A special feature of her insurance under-taking is comprehensive policies for Cinemas.
WOMAN WELO KEEPS THE UNITED STATES NAVY IN FIGHTING TRIM.

Miss Rose Savage, of the United States Navy Department, is seen with the large chart which is used to record the efficiency of the United States fleet. She keeps tract of every vessel, keeping a record of all repairs made, the length of time between trips, the location of the vessels, the condition of the ship when last in Navy Yard, and the time when it is due in Navy Yard for inspection, thereby maintaining the highest possible efficiency at all times.
JEUNE FILLE ANGLAISE FAISANT LE SERVICE D'un MOBILI

A number of women who log for the healthy open air life of the Colonies, are being trained at Fokkerin, where a fare, based on Colonial ideas, has been started by the Ron Rupert Guiness. The women are taught toxy everything connected with the life on a Colonial farm. A couple of pretty pupils feeding the fowls.

A party of merry faced women, in jerseys short skirts and lo gings, have created a big stir at certain Essexz Farms, where they are employed to replace farmhands who have answered their country's call. These women are working on the land out of sheer a trictosis, and doing it unnecessarily well. They look after the feeding of the cattle, clean out the cowsheds, and do all kinds of farm work.
This girl farmer does not mind a land of hay.

There are two occupations that predominate the activities of the people in war time. The men are fighters, and most of the women are either farming or preparing to raise crops for at least their own household.
The raising of sufficiently large crops to feed the United States and the allies, is one of the biggest problems of the moment.

A bill is up in Congress asking for conscription of farm workers so that the output will be at least normal. The woman want to be considered as factors, and are anxious to be just as busy tiling the soil, as the men.

A number of women are studying farming at the New York State School of Agriculture at Farmingdals, Long Island, so that they will be able to teach the people how to cultivate every inch of their gardens and raise enough necessary vegetables to supply their own families. In this way the crops of the country can be diverted in a large measure to the other side and it will at the same time out the coast of living.

Mrs. Raymond Brown, Chairman of organization for the New York State Women Suffrage Party, is well known as a perfect house-keeper and she has written magazine articles on "Systematic Housekeeping." Mrs. Brown is shown at work in her kitchen. Mrs. Brown is doing her share in getting house- keepers to sign the Hoover food pledge and follow the regulations. The New York State Women Suffrage Party has distributed throughout the state over one hundred thousand food conservation pledges. (SOCIAL REGISTER) 8/2/17.
Mrs: Frank A. Vanderlip, wife of the well known banker, and chairman of the Twelfth Campaign District of the New York State Woman Suffrage Party, at work in her kitchen.
Mrs. Vanderlip has installed in her summer home "Beechwood" in Scarborough, a complete system of food conservation in which her entire household is cooperating.

Mrs. Vanderlip has helped greatly in the distribution of over a hundred thousand food pledges sent broadcast over New York State by the Woman Suffrage Party.

CIRCUMFERENCE CIRCUMFERENCE CIRCUMFERENCE

In XXWA row of quaint little white cottages built on land the title of which dates back to Revolutionary times, young women are now playing the needle, patching, felling, quilting. There are some twenty women and girls who are earning their living making the same kinds of quilts and coverlets their great-grandmothers used to make. As this is the twentieth century, they have put a few modern touches to the industry, the most noted of which are their rigid eight hour working law, and a regulation earning wage.

The quilting Bee,as the little cottage factory is named,was established three years ago to give congennial employment to the women and girls of Rye,N.Y.,who needed it and to revive the art of quilting. The quilting Bee was incorporated last year and now has become self-supporting, and before long the turstoes hope to make it a paying business.
The young girls XXX seen in the photograph are being educated in the art of the plain and fancy sewing, and are seen embroidering a baby guilt, stretched on a frame to keep it taut.

ONE DON'T MIND WAITING FOR ELEVATOR WHEN RUN BY THIS CHARMING LIFT "BOY."
Miss Helen Egan, elevator"boy", ready to close the gates and send her car upward in the Donald Court. Appointments, 179th St., and Broadway. N.Y.

This apartment house is one of the first to start the vogue for girl elevator "boys". It is considered a success so far and not a complaint has been registered against their service.

The elevator girls have made themselves with all the controls and apparatus and are not shooting dice while the buzzer ticks until worn out. They are right on the job, polite, MHK and efficient. They will show "mere man" that they can hold down his job in this particular capacity and allow him to shoulder a gun for his country.

The "longshoregirls" arrived in their blue overalls and caps look hardy and fit. The girls are leaning how to drive trolley cars, locomotives, electric winches, oranges, derricks and other machinery in use on docks in loading vessels. The photos were taken at the Bush Terminal Company docks in Brooklyn. FIRST WOMAN IN COUNTRY TO GET RADIO LICENSE: OFFERS SERVICES TO GOVERNMENT.
Miss Margaret M. A. Donahus of Boston Satga at her radio machines.

This young lady is, upon the best information, the first woman in the United States to get a first class commercial radio operator's license. In a letter to Captain H. C. Gawler, federal radio inspector, she said that she would accept active duty in any branch of the service. At present she is employed by a private film in Boston as a telegraph operator. She has always been interested in radio work and took it up at a Boston radio school.

The US of women radio operators to man the shore stations which will be operated by the Navy department in connection with the power boat and submarine chasing dealers is contemplated by naval officials said an officer today. Thirty-five women have already volunteered their services in this capacity.

LADY BOOTBLACK MAKES APPEARANCE IN RANKS OF WOMEN-WORKERS.

The bootblack, though a man of humble occupation has proven quite as ardent a patriarch as many men in higher stations and when the call is sent out, any shoe-shining stands will be found without their "Tony's" and "Joes" and "Franks."

Despite this patriotic exhibition by our nights of the brush and cloth, one must have their shoes shined and if our man has gone to shoulder a gun, why we will be just as pleased to have a flair Miss do the honors. The McAlpin Hotel, N.Y., has, we are led to believe, introduced the first lady bootblack and she can certainly put a mirror-like polish on shoes. She has a neat cozy little "shoe-shine" parlor and needless to say always has a line waiting for she also has men customers. She has been so busy since the innovation went into effect that she will very soon have to have an assistant to help her out.
Photograph shows Miss Cecillia Swain, first lady bootblask at work in her "shoe shining parlor" in the Hotel McAlpix N.Y.
Women employed in building streets.

The example of the Prussian Railroad Management who have been employing women for some time past on the Railroad beds, for scarcity of men willing to work at the low wages, has now been imitated by the Municipal Governments of some of the Berlin suburbs. Therefore squads of women may be seen working sometimes alone and sometimes hand in hand with men, levelling the ground and shovelling dirt to lay out new streets. These women are all from the upper part of Silesia, they talk mostly Polish although they understand German, and they are paid at the rate of 35 Pfenning an hour which seems high wages to them.
